details:
What it does and how it works
Astro Health is a crew health monitor that runs on a real wrist watch. It tells an astronaut what to do about their health when the flight surgeon on Earth cannot answer in time. The system has three parts that work today:

  1. Watch app. A Garmin Connect IQ app on a fenix 5 runs a 2-minute daily check: resting heart rate (30 s still), mood, sleep, symptoms, cabin CO2 and a 5-trial reaction test modeled on NASA’s Reaction Self Test. Body Scan adds heart rate variability (RMSSD), breathing rate, gravity in g and motion. Advice appears on the wrist with no phone needed.
  2. Cloud sync. Each check becomes one JSON record in Firebase Realtime Database. If there is no link, records wait in a queue on the watch and retry every 30 seconds until they get through. That fits missions with long communication gaps.
  3. Crew app. An offline-first Progressive Web App turns the data into a Mission Readiness score from 0 to 100 built from 7 signals, plus 3 concrete actions for today. It also shows trends, the 5 NASA hazards with the person’s own numbers, and a 7-day report for the flight surgeon.

The scoring is an open rules engine, not a black box. The weights are: sleep 25, HRV 15, resting heart rate 15, reaction time 15, cabin CO2 10, mood and stress 10, symptoms 10. HRV, heart rate and reaction time are compared with the person’s own 14-day median, not with a population average. Red flags such as vision changes (SANS), chest pain or low SpO2 cap the score at 33. Mission profiles change the guidance: on the ISS the app says to call the flight surgeon now, while on a Mars transit it says to start the onboard protocol, because a reply from Earth can take up to 40 minutes.

Use of NASA data
Every rule comes from the challenge resources. The 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight became one card per hazard, each with personal status. Each card links to the official HRP Risks. The design follows ongoing HRP research: ARCHeR on Artemis II (a wrist device plus well-being surveys) and Standard Measures. The CSA radiation article drives the daily dose log against the 600 mSv career limit. Hard limits come from NASA standards: CO2 at 3 mmHg (NASA-STD-3001) and 8.5 h of planned sleep.

Benefits and intended impact
On Moon and Mars missions, crews will face communication delays and less access to emergency medical help. Astro Health moves the first decision onto the astronaut’s wrist. It explains every score, so both the crew and the flight surgeon can check the reasoning. On Earth, the same tool fits people far from a doctor: polar stations, ships, remote mines and rural clinics. It is low cost, because it uses watches people already own, the free Firebase tier and open web technology.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Hardware: Garmin fenix 5 and Forerunner 735XT watches, with an Android phone running Garmin Connect as the Bluetooth bridge.
  • Watch: Monkey C with the Garmin Connect IQ SDK, the FIT file format and Garmin’s official FIT SDK for tests. There is also a Wear OS build in Java.
  • Cloud: Firebase Realtime Database REST API, with security rules that allow append-only writes per crew code.
  • Crew app: HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript as a PWA with a service worker for offline use, hosted on GitHub Pages.
  • Testing: Node.js unit tests, a Python mock of Firebase for offline and retry tests, and end-to-end UI tests in headless Chrome with Playwright.

How it is creative
Most health dashboards run on invented data. Ours is a working pipeline on real hardware: a real check on a fenix 5 travels through Firebase and appears in the app with the same values. The watch works standalone, at the edge, with no phone or link. XP is earned for logging, never for good numbers, so hiding a symptom does not pay. Finally, the app does more than show numbers: it links signals to a cause. For example, a headache, short sleep and slower reactions together with rising CO2 lead to one action: check the scrubber and fans.

Factors we considered

  • Communication delays and outages, which is why there is an offline queue and the app works without a network.
  • Old, low-power watches with limited memory, which is why the check fits in 2 minutes and the records are small.
  • Honest self-reporting, which is why XP rewards logging rather than good results.
  • Transparency for crew and doctors, which is why the rules are open and every rule cites its source.
  • Privacy, which is why the Firebase rules restrict data to each crew’s code.
  • Honest limits: this is a prototype, not a medical device. The thresholds come from NASA sources but are not clinically validated, and the demo mission data is simulated.

  • Live crew app: https://qudaibergent.github.io/AstroHealth/
